hints: Start by sorting the two waves in the question: light as a transverse electromagnetic wave and sound in air as a longitudinal mechanical wave.
Recall which wave needs a material medium to travel and which wave properties such as diffraction are shared by all progressive waves.
Recall the condition for the Doppler effect - relative motion of source and observer - and check if it depends on being transverse, longitudinal, or needing a vacuum.
walkthrough: Identify the two waves: light waves are transverse electromagnetic waves with speed about $3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ in vacuum, and sound waves in air are longitudinal mechanical waves needing a medium.
Check diffraction: all waves spread when passing through a gap or around an obstacle of similar size to wavelength $\lambda$, so both light and sound can be diffracted.

Check transverse-longitudinal and vacuum statements: sound oscillations are parallel to energy transfer so it is longitudinal and cannot travel in vacuum, while light oscillations of $E$ and $B$ fields are perpendicular to travel so it is transverse and can travel in vacuum.

Check the Doppler effect: for any wave with speed $v$, relative motion of source and observer changes the observed wavelength and frequency, heard as pitch change for sound and seen as red-shift or blue-shift for light.
Therefore only the statement that both show the Doppler effect is correct. This is option A.

options.A: Both types show an observed change in frequency or wavelength when source and observer have relative motion along the line joining them.
options.B: Diffraction is a property of all waves, and sound with its longer wavelength is often diffracted strongly around everyday obstacles.
options.C: The types are reversed: sound in air is longitudinal with oscillations parallel to travel, while light is transverse electromagnetic.
options.D: The vacuum requirement is reversed: light can travel through vacuum but sound needs particles of a medium to transmit compressions and rarefactions.
